Chapter 4: Supporting Growth and Ownership
When you think about what really sets great managers apart, it’s not just their ability to listen or give feedback. What truly makes a difference is how they support the growth and ownership of their team members.
It’s about creating real opportunities—chances for people to stretch, learn, and take on meaningful work that actually matters. Now, instead of holding the reins tightly and controlling every move, the best leaders empower their teams. They encourage others to step up and lead in their own way.
So, how do you support growth? Well, it all starts with understanding each person’s goals, their unique strengths, and the areas where they can still develop. This takes ongoing conversations and a genuine effort to spot potential—even when it hasn’t fully emerged yet.
Think of yourself like a coach: you’re there to help folks set clear goals, find the right resources, and work through challenges as they come. Let’s talk about ownership for a second. Here, it’s all about giving people a real sense of agency and accountability. When you trust someone with important tasks—when you let them make decisions and actually see the impact of their work—they become way more invested in the team’s success.
Looking for practical ways to encourage growth and ownership? Here are a few ideas:
Give people meaningful projects, not just the usual routine work.
Ask employees to come up with solutions and take initiative.
Offer access to training, mentorship, or fresh experiences.
And don’t forget to celebrate progress and learning—even if things don’t turn out perfectly. Let me give you a quick example. Imagine a marketing manager who notices someone on their team has a real knack for creative problem-solving. Instead of keeping that person boxed into a narrow role, the manager invites them to lead an entirely new campaign. Sure, there’s guidance, but there’s also plenty of freedom to make independent decisions. The result? That team member steps up, learns new skills, and gains serious confidence. The team gets fresh ideas, and the manager has more time to focus on the big-picture strategy. Of course, growth isn’t just about the wins. When someone stumbles, it’s the perfect moment for a manager to step in—not to assign blame, but to help them unpack what happened, learn from it, and try again.
That way, mistakes become stepping stones, not setbacks. Here’s something to keep in mind: a culture of growth and ownership doesn’t just happen on its own. It takes real intention and a willingness to let go of the urge to control every little detail. But when managers adopt this mindset, teams become stronger, more adaptable, and a whole lot more creative. So, here’s the key takeaway—supporting growth and ownership is one of the most powerful ways to lift others up. It shifts the manager’s role from gatekeeper to enabler, unlocking the full potential of every team member.
When people are trusted to lead, they almost always rise to the occasion—and that’s when the entire organization wins.
